rules_text:
Rules summary ON YOUR TURN You have two options: 1. Take Supplies - Choose an inkwell and take all supplies from it. - Supplies must be placed on matching spaces on your page during the same turn. - Taking supplies from a diamond also gives you its Technique card. Add it to your Workspace. - You must be able to place everything you take. 2. Turn Your Page - Score your current page and receive a new one. - Your turn ends. PLACING & SCORING - Cubes must go on matching spaces. - Gold cubes can go anywhere. - ? spaces accept any color. - Cubes cannot be moved once placed. - Completed illustrations score their indicated points. - Incomplete illustrations score 0 points. - Filling the multiplier space gives extra points for cubes of that color, including cubes on incomplete illustrations. - Gold counts as every color and works with every multiplier. TURNING THE PAGE When you turn your page: - Score completed illustrations, the multiplier, and your Workspace ability. - Flip the current page face-down. - Return your cubes to the appropriate supplies. - Choose the next available page. - If you chose to turn voluntarily, take a gold cube and immediately place it on the new page. - Move your Techniques below your Workspace. They remain active, but your Workspace becomes available for new Techniques. REFILLING THE BOARD When an entire inkwell type is empty: - Advance the Abbot. - Add 1 common cube to each inkwell that still contains supplies. - Refill completely empty inkwells and Technique spaces according to the setup rules. TECHNIQUES - Techniques are optional abilities that can alter gameplay. - They may be used immediately unless specified otherwise. - Some Techniques are one-time effects. - Others remain active. THE ABBOT - When the Abbot crosses an arrow, players who have not yet turned the indicated page are forced to turn it on their next turn. - Forced turns do not provide the bonus gold cube. END GAME - When someone turns their Page III, the end game begins. - Players who have finished their pages score 3 points instead of taking another turn. - They also advance the Abbot when possible. - The game ends when everyone has turned their final page or the Abbot crosses the final arrow. - The player with the highest score wins. - Ties go to the player who turned their Page III first.

---

The abbey at Iona is famed for its illustrious manuscripts, replete with gold leaf and remarkable calligraphy. In fact, through talent and discipline, you have joined their ranks as a master illuminator!

In Inkwell, each player will either take supplies from a shared mat, or choose to score and move on to a new page of their own codex. Supplies include colored ink cubes, gold leaf, and technique cards with special powers and effects. Everything you take must fit on your manuscript card, and if you empty the last inkwell of a certain type, the abbot ticks down the game time towards ending the game. If you choose to turn the page, you score for all your completed work, and collect your ability cards on the side to benefit you the rest of the game, building an 'engine' of learned skills. You also get a reward of gold leaf and a chance to pick your next page to work on. Just beware that if the abbot becomes upset, he may force you to move forward before you are finished.

A strategic and tactical game with few rules and lots of choices, Inkwell is designed to celebrate beautiful historical manuscripts and surprisingly tricky gameplay for groups or even solo play.

—description from the publisher
community_text:
[Rating: 3/10] So boring. The theme is not integrated with the gameplay at all. The art isn't even on the side of the card you use! There are no interesting choices or mechanics. It's just pulling annoyingly tiny blocks out of a bag that's too small to mix them up properly and then putting these blocks on a visually messy card sized 'page'.  There is no element that provokes delight here except for the few brass cubes perhaps but they are just wilds that make the other cubes feel insubstantial and even more boring than their primary colours appear. Gold painted wooden cubes would suffice though probably then

[Rating: 4/10] Efficiency puzzle where it is hard to meaningfully catch up on someone who is having fortuitously an early lead... not much interaction at all apart from hate drafting.

[Rating: 4.5/10] Pretty bog standard. Shares dna with Harmonies but has none of the spacial puzzle considerations. Simply fill in your pages and move on. The player powers add a little bit of interest but there's not much here. Can't believe it took three designers to come up with this.

[Rating: 5/10] Lovely package with impressive art. Pacing is interesting but the puzzle is lackluster. Too derivative of Azul but not nearly as dynamic.

[Rating: 5/10] We way underestimated how much the rules themselves would hustle us along in this new DVC release -- nobody ever turned their page voluntarily, the abbot always made us do it. If leaving a page early is strategically viable (I assume it is) then we missed some of the game's depth. And pages of the same level seemed to reward different colors of cube, so when we were all in sync, my first choice in the offer was rarely anyone else's, etc. That made it feel less Azulish and more Cascadian, which is not my preferred mode of take-and-make.  [1 play]

[Rating: 5/10] Gorgeous and simple. Didn't personally get my blood pumping but it's a very short game with low stakes and easy to whip out for a non-gamer audience surely :)

[Rating: 5/10] There's not really much here to set it apart from others game that do similar things. The bonus abilities you get along the way can be quite useful and the thing that winds up setting you apart from other players.

[Rating: 5.5/10] I want to like it but it's more of an efficiency game than a puzzle. You can basically fill all of your pages if you don't make dumb decisions so it's more a matter of who gets the best tokens aligning with their scoring options.

[Rating: 6/10] Scream Park by DVC is great. This is mid. Lots of rule breaking powers (techniques) to track. Feels like solo goal score is a bridge too far. I was looking forward to this release and I'm a bit let down. Probably trade this one on.

[Rating: 6/10] Inkwell is a cube-drafting and cube-placing game that calls to mind former titles like Azul, Sagrada, and Illumination, although here the pressure is slight and the gameplay is consistently gentle. At its best, it offers a perspective that's more process-oriented than puzzly, its monks blending commercial and artistic pursuits as they hone their skills.  Read my review here: https://spacebiff.com/2026/04/02/inkwell/

[Rating: 6/10] It looks great, but I wish there was more to the gameplay or scoring that I could latch on too. I've only played with 2 players and those games have had an almost identical arc, with the differentiator being the asymmetric player powers allowing for slightly more scoring.  I'll give it another couple of plays with more players to see if there is something else there.

[Rating: 6/10] I appreciate the form factor of DVC’s recent lineup, and Inkwell with its cloth mat, stylized old art, and painting/recipe fulfillment gameplay caught my eye. The demo pitched this as Azul meets Sagrada, and while the “take all cubes from a round tray” does have the Azul mechanic this feels like Fresco with friendlier gameplay. As you complete art pieces and flip your manuscript powers become unlocked to add velocity to the rounds.
